rows: Severe, 'boring' pain; may radiate to temple/jaw; awakens patient at night
Deep red, bluish, or violaceous hue
Exquisitely tender to touch through lids
Strongly associated with systemic autoimmune disease (up to 50%)

branches: Posterior Scleritis (Involves globe behind insertion of recti)

sections.title: The Phenylephrine Blanch Test
content: Step 1: Observe the baseline congestion and vessel color in natural light.
Step 2: Instill one drop of Phenylephrine 2.5% into the affected eye.
Step 3: Wait 10-15 minutes for the vasoconstrictive effect.
Step 4: Re-evaluate: If vessels whiten, it's Episcleritis. If they remain dark/congested, suspect Scleritis.

sections.title: Scleritis Red Flags
content: Necrotizing Scleritis: The most severe form, often associated with systemic vasculitis.
Scleral Thinning: Appearance of the dark uvea through the thinned sclera (Scleromalacia Perforans).
Vision Loss: Potential for permanent damage due to uveitis, glaucoma, or keratitis.
Exudative Retinal Detachment: A serious complication of Posterior Scleritis.

sections.title: Vessel Mobility Details
content: In Episcleritis, the inflamed vessels can be moved over the underlying sclera with a cotton-tipped applicator.
In Scleritis, the inflammation is deep within the sclera; the vessels are fixed and do not move independently of the globe.
Episcleritis usually resolves within 1-3 weeks without treatment.
Scleritis requires urgent systemic workup and aggressive anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapy.
